knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 2.4.2
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly extracts moments from an MGF?
knowledge_checks.body: Select the derivative and Taylor-coefficient rule.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Raw moments are derivatives at zero, or equivalently factorial-scaled Taylor coefficients.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Stopping at the MGF definition or evaluating the derivative at the wrong point.

choices.label: If M_X(t) exists around zero, its Taylor expansion has E[X^r] as the coefficient multiplied by r!, equivalently M_X^{(r)}(0)=E[X^r].
M_X(0)=E[X], so evaluating the MGF once at zero gives the first moment.
M_X'(1)=E[X] for every distribution because moments are evaluated at t=1.
Writing M_X(t)=E[e^{tX}] completes moment extraction without differentiation or coefficient matching.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 2.4.2
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. For Poisson X, M_X(t)=exp(λ(e^t-1)). Which statement correctly obtains E[X]?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Differentiate using the chain rule and set t=0. The value M(0)=1 is normalisation, not the mean.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Using M(0) as the mean or writing the MGF without extracting a derivative.

choices.label: M_X(0)=1, so E[X]=1 for every Poisson distribution.
M_X'(0)=e^λ because differentiating removes the inner e^t-1 term.
The formula M_X(t)=E[e^{tX}] already states the mean, so no derivative is needed.
